background.definition: Diabetic retinopathy is a specific microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus occurring in 2 stages, nonproliferative and proliferative (). Diabetic macular edema can occur at any stage of retinopathy and is characterized by increased vascular permeability leading to deposition of hard exudates at the central retina.

list.listitem: Diabetic retinopathy is rare in preadolescent children and during the first 3 to 5 years of type 1 diabetes.

In patients with type 2 diabetes and no baseline eye disease, the yearly incidence of sight-threatening retinopathy is 0.3% in the first year after onset of diabetes, rising progressively to 1.8% in the fifth year, with a cumulative 5-year incidence of 3.9%.
The prevalence of retinopathy correlates strongly with the duration of diabetes.
After 20 years of diabetes, nearly all patients with type 1 diabetes and more than 80% with type 2 diabetes have some degree of retinopathy.
Among diabetic adults 40 years and older in the US, 40% have retinopathy and 8% have sight-threatening retinopathy.
Diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of new blindness among adults 20 to 74 years of age.
The presence of proliferative retinopathy in type 2 diabetics is associated with increased all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, and coronary heart disease.
Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

In the earliest stages of retinopathy, retinal vessels develop microaneurysms and hemorrhage into the retina. Vascular damage and occlusion lead to retinal ischemia, prompting the growth of new blood vessels on the retinal surface in an attempt to maintain retinal blood supply. However, the newly formed vessels are prone to bleeding, which leads to vitreous hemorrhage progressing to fibrosis and tractional retinal detachment.
Diabetic macular edema is caused by microvascular damage leading to increased permeability of retinal vessels, which in turn leak exudative material, resulting in retinal thickening.
Type 1 diabetes: dilated, comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years of onset of diabetes followed by annual eye examinations.C
Type 2 diabetes: dilated, comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of diagnosis of diabetes; if initially normal, can have eye exams every 2 years. B
Optimal glycemic control reduces the risk and progression of retinopathy. B
Intensive blood pressure control over 5 years reduces the onset but not the progression of diabetic retinopathy among patients with T2DM with hypertension. A

Type 1 diabetes: dilated, comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years of onset of diabetes followed by annual eye examinations. However, 30-year follow-up of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) suggested that persons with no or mild retinopathy have a low (<5%) risk of progression to proliferative retinopathy over 3 years, while persons with moderate or severe retinopathy may require more frequent examinations. Tailoring examination frequency to retinopathy severity reduced the overall number of examinations by 58% without worsening visual outcomes.
Type 2 diabetes: dilated, comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of diagnosis of diabetes; if initially normal, can have eye exams every 2 years.
In the patient with type 2 diabetes and a normal eye exam, less frequent exams may be considered at an interval of 2 to 3 years.

Digital retinal photography with review by experienced ophthalmologists is an alternative method of screening, especially in areas lacking access to qualified ophthalmologists. Teleretinal screening is another useful way to improve diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy where access is limited.

In patients with type 1 diabetes, the rate of retinopathy was 1.2% per year in patients treated with tight glycemic control (HgbA1C <7%) compared with the rate of 4.7% per year in those treated with usual care (NNT = 29).

In patients with type 2 diabetes, the rate of laser treatment in patients with tight glycemic control was 7.9 per 1000 person-years compared with 11 per 1000 person-years in those treated with usual care (NNT = 323).

In patients with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, 8% of those patients with tight blood pressure control (target blood pressure <150/85 mm Hg) required photocoagulation compared with 12% of those with less tight control (NNT = 25; 95% CI, 13-240).

More importantly, vision loss occurred in 2.4% of patients with tight blood pressure control compared with 3.1% of the less tight control patients (NNT = 200 for 5 years) and were less likely to have deterioration (NNT = 8).
A Cochrane review found intensive blood pressure control over 5 years reduces the onset of diabetic retinopathy among patients with T2DM with hypertension.

Patients with type 1 diabetes and existing mild to moderate nonproliferative retinopathy treated with tight glycemic control were less likely to develop retinopathy (3.7% per year vs 7.8%; NNT = 24), develop severe proliferative or nonproliferative retinopathy (1.1% per year vs 2.3%; NNT = 84), or require laser treatment (0.9% per year vs 2.3%; NNT = 72) than patients receiving usual care.

Patients with type 2 diabetes treated with tight glycemic control and a fibrate were less likely to progress on a 17-point diabetic retinopathy scale, but were equally likely to develop moderate vision loss as patients receiving usual care more than 5 years of follow-up.

Aspirin therapy does not prevent the progression of retinopathy, nor is it contraindicated for prevention of cardiovascular disease in the presence of retinopathy, as it does not increase the risk of retinal hemorrhage.
A Cochrane review found intensive blood pressure control over 5 years does not reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy among patients with T2DM with hypertension.

The initial eye examination should include slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated funduscopy including stereoscopic examination of the posterior pole, and examination of the peripheral retina and vitreous. C
Single field fundus photography is an option for patients who cannot access an ophthalmologist or optometrist. B
Vitreous hemorrhage is a complication of retinopathy and may present with sudden unilateral vision loss.
However, in most cases retinopathy is asymptomatic until it progresses to its end stages characterized by visual loss.

The American Academy of Ophthalmology guidelines recommend that a comprehensive initial eye examination for the patient with known or suspected diabetic retinopathy include visual acuity, intraocular pressure, gonioscopy when indicated, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated funduscopy including stereoscopic examination of the posterior pole, and examination of the peripheral retina and vitreous.

Single field fundus photography may be considered as an option in patients who cannot access an ophthalmologist or optometrist; when compared with 7-field stereophotography, it is between 61% to 90% sensitive and 85% to 97% specific. When compared with dilated ophthalmoscopy by an ophthalmologist, single-field fundus photography has sensitivity from 38% to 100% and specificity from 75 % to 100%.
In diagnosing diabetic macular edema, optical coherence tomography is reasonably sensitive (0.79; 95% CI, 0.71-0.86) and specific (0.88; 95% CI, 0.80-0.93).
summarizes the identification and follow-up of patients with diabetic retinopathy.
Refer patients with macular edema, severe nonproliferative retinopathy, or any degree of proliferative retinopathy to an ophthalmologist immediately for treatment. C

Laser photocoagulation reduces the risk of vision loss in patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy, clinically significant macular edema, and some cases of severe nonproliferative retinopathy. B

Aspirin therapy does not prevent the progression of retinopathy, nor is it contraindicated for prevention of cardiovascular disease in the presence of retinopathy, as it does not increase the risk of retinal hemorrhage. A

Anti-angiogenesis therapy with anti-vascular endothelial growth factors (anti-VEGF) such as aflibercept, bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and brolucizumab is associated with better one year outcomes in patients with diabetic macular edema compared to laser photocoagulation. A strategy of observation and using an anti-VEGF only if vision worsens is reasonable. B

Anti-VEGF plus panretinal photocoagulation (PRP), compared to PRP alone, may produce nonclinically meaningful improvement in visual acuity, regression of new vessels, and may reduce vitreous hemorrhage and need for vitrectomy. B

Perioperative use of anti-VEGF prior to vitrectomy decreases early (<4 weeks) and late (≥4 weeks) postoperative vitreous cavity hemorrhage (POVCH) among patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy, A and may improve visual outcomes. B

Use of fenofibrate can reduce the need for photocoagulation in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (NNT = 67 for 5 years; NNT = 17 for patients with retinopathy at baseline).A Cochrane review, based on data from 1 study with 208 participants, found that among patients with T2DM with overt retinopathy, fenofibrate may prevent the progression of retinopathy.
There is no evidence for or against use of pentoxifylline for treatment of diabetic retinopathy. A systematic review found no adequate quality trials.

Anti-angiogenesis therapy with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) modalities (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, brolucizumab, and aflibercept) is associated with both an improved chance of gaining vision, and a reduced chance of losing vision compared to laser photocoagulation. In terms of absolute benefit, use of anti-VEGF therapy is associated with 18 more people with improved vision per 100 treated compared to photocoagulation. Visual outcomes appear comparable for anti-VEGF drugs at 24 months. Based on low- to very low-certainty evidence, anti-VEGF drugs to not appear to increase all-cause mortality.

A RCT randomized 660 adults with diabetic macular edema to aflibercept, bevacizumab, or ranibizumab. Outcomes were similar for patients with initially mild visual defect, but aflibercept was more effective in patients with initially worse visual acuity.

A Cochrane review evaluating 28 RCTs found perioperative use of anti-VEGF prior to vitrectomy for patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy decreases early (<4 weeks) and late (≥4 weeks) postoperative vitreous cavity hemorrhage (POVCH), based on moderate- and high-certainty evidence, respectively. They may also lead to better visual outcomes, based on low-certainty evidence.

In patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes with proliferative retinopathy, panretinal photocoagulation reduces severe visual loss (best acuity 5/200 or worse) from 15.9% to 6.4% at 2 years (NNT = 11).

In patients with neovascularization at the optic disk or vitreous hemorrhage, the benefit of panretinal photocoagulation is greatest: progression to severe visual loss decreased from 26% to 11% in treated patients at 2 years (NNT = 7).

A Cochrane review noted that anti-VEGF plus panretinal photocoagulation (PRP), compared to PRP alone, may produce nonclinically meaningful improvement in visual acuity, regression of new vessels, and may reduce vitreous hemorrhage and need for vitrectomy. It is uncertain if anti-VEGF plus PRP cause more or less adverse events than PRP alone, but the combined treatment likely does not affect quality of life.
Early vitrectomy within 6 months after recent vitreous hemorrhage causing impaired visual acuity to less than 5/200 improves significant visual recovery from 15% to 25% (NNT = 10).
For patients with type 2 diabetes who develop severe nonproliferative retinopathy, laser photocoagulation decreases risk of severe visual loss and vitrectomy by 50%.

In patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who develop macular edema, focal laser photocoagulation decreases the 2-year progression to doubling of the visual angle from 20% to 8%. Intravitreal steroids may be helpfulas well as intravitreal bevacizumab or intravitreal ranibizumab.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence regarding the comparative efficacy and safety of argon laser and other modern laser techniques and modalities.
Vitrectomy should be considered in cases of macular edema with vitreous traction.

A study randomized 702 patients with diabetic macular edema to intravitreous aflibercept, laser photocoagulation followed by aflibercept if vision worsened, or observation with aflibercept if vision worsened. Outcomes were similar, so a conservative strategy of observation followed by aflibercept only if vision worsens is reasonable.

In a randomized trial that initially enrolled 277 participants with proliferative diabetic retinopathy, of whom 184 were present at 5 years, intravitreous ranibizumab was similar to panretinal photocoagulation.
There is insufficient evidence for herbal medicine to treat diabetic retinopathy.
Patients with diabetes should be routinely referred to an ophthalmologist or optometrist for dilated, comprehensive eye examinations.
Refer patients with macular edema, severe nonproliferative retinopathy, or any degree of proliferative retinopathy to an ophthalmologist immediately for treatment.
There is no evidence of an association between dietary vitamin C, vitamin E, or magnesium intake (or plasma levels) and diabetic retinopathy.

A meta-analysis found no association between semaglutide and an overall increased risk of eye disorders, including diabetic retinopathy. While semaglutide may increase the risk of NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy), the number of events is low and the confidence interval for the NNTH is wide. Therefore, the clinical significance of this association remains imprecise.

Prognostic factors for the development and progression of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in people with diabetic retinopathy include poor glycemic control, renal impairment, younger age at diagnosis of diabetes, high triglyceride levels, and increased retinal venular diameters. B

In patients with type 2 diabetes, background retinopathy progresses to sight-threatening retinopathy at a rate of 5% per year. In patients with mild preproliferative retinopathy, this rate increases to 15% per year. B
In patients with type 2 diabetes with a normal initial dilated eye exam, only 0.3% developed sight-threatening retinopathy 1 year later. B
In the presence of retinopathy, more frequent follow-up may be required as guided by the ophthalmologist. C
Pregnancy may exacerbate retinopathy in patients with type 1 diabetes.
When planning pregnancy, women with preexisting diabetes should have a baseline comprehensive eye examination and should be counseled regarding the risk of developing retinopathy.

Pregnant women should have a comprehensive eye examination during the first trimester of pregnancy, and should have close opththalmologic follow-up throughout pregnancy and during the first year following delivery.
In general, screening for diabetic eye disease is not necessary in patients less than 10 years of age, as retinopathy is rare before adolescence.
